citeAs: Rajpurkar, P., Zhang, J., Lopyrev, K., and Liang, P. (2016). SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. EMNLP 2016.
creator: Pranav Rajpurkar, Jian Zhang, Konstantin Lopyrev, Percy Liang (Stanford University)
description: SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text (span) from the corresponding reading passage. Questions were posed by crowdworkers, and the dataset features a diverse range of question and answer types requiring various forms of reasoning.
name: SQuAD (Stanford Question Answering Dataset)
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in the development and test sets (1 original + at least 2 additional answers)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers located in the United States or Canada, with a 97% HIT acceptance rate and a minimum of 1000 HITs completed on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was assessed using inter-annotator agreement: the second answer to each question was treated as the human prediction, with other answers as ground truth. Human performance on the test set was 77.0% exact match and 86.8% F1. Mismatch occurred mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform (with Amazon Mechanical Turk as backend)
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada. Workers spent 4 minutes per paragraph, paid $9/hour. On each paragraph, workers asked and answered up to 5 questions; answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph. Workers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words, with copy-paste from the paragraph disabled. For additional answers, workers selected the shortest span answering each question, or marked it unanswerable.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in three stages: (1) passage curation from top-ranked English Wikipedia articles, (2) crowdsourcing question-answer pairs on those passages via the Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as backend, and (3) collecting additional answers for development and test sets.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Top 10,000 English Wikipedia articles ranked by Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks, from which 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random, yielding 23,215 paragraphs after filtering.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: Answers are constrained to be spans from the passage, which is more restrictive than free-form answers. 77.3% of correct answers are constituents in the constituency parse, placing an effective ceiling on accuracy of span-based methods. 2.6% of questions in development and test sets were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Wikipedia articles were filtered to the top 10,000 by PageRank; 536 were sampled at random. Individual paragraphs were extracted, stripping images, figures, and tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. Articles were partitioned randomly into training (80%), development (10%), and test (10%) sets.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive progress toward natural language understanding and reading comprehension in machines. It provides a large-scale benchmark that can spur development of more expressive models, with the long-term goal of machines that can read and understand text.
rai:dataUseCases: Reading comprehension and question answering research; training and evaluating machine learning models for natural language understanding; benchmarking progress toward human-level reading comprehension.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford CoreNLP (constituency parses, POS tags, NER tags) used to automatically categorize answer types; dependency parse trees used to measure syntactic divergence between questions and answer sentences.

evidence.name: We present the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), a new reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles
evidence.description: SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles, and is almost two orders of magnitude larger than previous manually labeled RC datasets such as MCTest

evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: we used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia's internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random. The result was 23,215 paragraphs for the 536 articles covering a wide range of topics
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada. Workers were asked to spend 4 minutes on every paragraph, and paid $9 per hour for the number of hours required to complete the article.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: To get an indication of human performance on SQuAD and to make our evaluation more robust, we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. The result was 23,215 paragraphs for the 536 articles covering a wide range of topics, from musical celebrities to abstract concepts. We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Towards the end goal of natural language understanding, we introduce the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, a large reading comprehension dataset on Wikipedia articles with crowdsourced question-answer pairs. We have made our dataset freely available to encourage exploration of more expressive models.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To evaluate human performance, we treat the second answer to each question as the human prediction, and keep the other answers as ground truth answers. The resulting human performance score on the test set is 77.0% for the exact match metric, and 86.8% for F1. Mismatch occurs mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: The non-numerical answers are categorized using constituency parses and POS tags generated by Stanford CoreNLP. The proper noun phrases are further split into person, location and other entities using NER tags.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: In contrast to prior datasets, SQuAD does not provide a list of answer choices for each question. Rather, systems must select the answer from all possible spans in the passage, thus needing to cope with a fairly large number of candidates. While questions with span-based answers are more constrained than the more interpretative questions found in more advanced standardized tests, we still find a rich diversity of questions and answer types in SQuAD.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: Ignoring punctuation and articles, we find that 77.3% of the correct answers in the development set are constituents. This places an effective ceiling on the accuracy of our methods.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Towards the end goal of natural language understanding, we introduce the Stanford Question Answering Dataset, a large reading comprehension dataset on Wikipedia articles with crowdsourced question-answer pairs. We have made our dataset freely available to encourage exploration of more expressive models.
